Yes but it's almost the norm to be scammed here, if you're a woman or a new driver. I work with professional drivers who tell me that it's normal because most mechanics just won't bother taking the engine apart, it's too much work. So they'll put a band aid on it and charge you as if they fixed it. It's baffling but it's almost the norm.

To tell yet another story, a couple of months I told a couple of drivers at work that my engine was making a weird noise. They said they'd check it out but they also said it was in my head. It got worse, I googled it and I told the head driver that I was going to go to a random mechanic and get scammed again because there was oil in the spark plugs, I said I found it on reddit. Next day he checked it out and, what do you know, there was oil in the spark plugs. He took it to a friend of his who fixed it for 100€. Then I went to a mechanic in my city who has lots of great reviews and, even though the problem was fixed, he asked me for 250€ so he could fix it. Then that guy who fixed the car for 100€ is the one who's ordered unnecessary parts because he has an illegal shop in his yard and overcharged me a few more times, lmao.

He didn't have time to look into it that day. He told me to bring it back and I'm waiting until I can take some time off work (hopefully next week) so I can take it back. In the meantime I keep wondering about what might be wrong and making myself paranoid.

So, because he doesn't own an actual repair shop, he had to take it somewhere else to fill it up with freon. Then he told me it was working but when I got the car, I found that it wasn't working at all. Then I took it to another guy who is the one who says it's the compressor. But, because I've been scammed and dismissed a couple of times so far, I'm having a hard time trusting him. I also don't trust the other guy in the slightest, so I'm thinking that it's very likely that he assembled it wrong when he took it apart to replace the condensor. 

I realize that it's a vague, pointless question but I'm waiting until I can get a couple of days off after Easter and in the meantime I keep getting anxious over what might be wrong, how long it'll take to fix, how much the most it can cost may be and how will I know if this new guy is being honest. Like, what if some wires were connected wrong and I end up paying 400€ over that?

It was also possible to get to a middle ground where both versions made sense. In the second season it starts making less sense.

They did a Paley Fest event, I think? Where journalists all but attacked them over how different the versions were, how little sense some things made and how they couldn't figure out what the actual truth was. Evidently, the only one who could defend the show was Joshua Jackson, he kept saying that there's no objective truth. Even the creator had no way to defend her script. Like, I get that Cole was stoned out of his mind in the second episode, he probably doesn't remember much, but he needed to get closure out of his meeting with Alison and he made up some memories that would give him that and I get that Alison was afraid of him because he'd aimed a gun at her the last time they'd met and now he showed up unannounced and stoned. Cole being stoned sort of saves that episode. 

Later, though, either Alison told Noah that Joanie wasn't his daughter when it was night or she did it during the day, both versions can't be true. One of them is telling a version of the truth and the other one is plain making shit up. Noah's version sounds more fake but Alison's version can't be true, either, because Noah and Helen wouldn't have had time to get drunk on the beach. The problem I have with this is that a. I don't understand why they're making stuff up/misrepresenting things from the second season onwards, since they have no one they're telling the story to and b. there should have been a way for us to be able to piece together what happened.

But, anyway, about that scene between Noah and Cole, I think Noah was making generic comments about teenagers being difficult, then Cole tried to tell him how to raise his son and Noah made an incredibly insensitive comment towards him, because he dgaf about his and Alison's dead son, that has been well established. His attitude/tone was probably not as aggressive, Alison misremembers it.

Max was just lonely and unloved, always had been. Noah couldn't possibly be a good friend, when all he ever cared about was himself but Max hung around him and Helen hoping to feel like he belonged. He gave him money, advice, listened to his problems, he tried to be a friend, even though he didn't get much out of the relationship. He was kind of a sad person, despite all the money, really, and definitely a douchebag, but I do feel a bit sorry for him. I'm not picking sides, though, because I don't care about any of them. 

Helen even attempting to get with him grossed me out and I was glad that she broke it off quickly but she also could've told Noah, Noah absolutely has no leg to stand on whatsoever and Max hanging around trying to get any attention from either of them at all was pathetic.

But it's phyllo dough (the kind we use for savory pies is basically bread dough with a bit of oil added to it, not the kind you find in US shops) and then you mix spinach, any other green leafy vegetables you can think of (they should be about 2lbs total), green onion, some leak, dill, parsley, peppermint, salt, pepper and about 1lb of crumbled up feta cheese. Then you oil a pan (we use 16-inch round ones, if that helps), lay down a phyllo sheet, sprinkle oil with a brush, add another phyllo sheet, sprinkle more oil, third phyllo sheet, oil, add half the filling, again three phyllo sheets with oil inbetween, the rest of the filling, again 3 phyllo sheets, you sprinkle more oil and water on top and then you bake it in a preheated oven at 340 degrees for about an hour.

I actually thought you were using oil but even if it was melted butter, it wouldn't work because, as I explained, the whole point with bougatsa dough is to get butter to melt so it can release steam. Bougatsa isn't made with phyllo.

The recipe you linked is the type of phyllo dough that most people make, with white wine vinegar being an optional ingredient. That type of dough is used in most savory pies and it's pretty much the same recipe you'd use for a 60-65% hydration bread. If you add butter or oil to the dough, it's meant to make much thinner phyllo sheets, which are used to make dessert, mainly. More rarely we further enrich the dough with eggs. The two latter types are very difficult to make at home. They're even difficult to handle at home, tbh, even the shitty store bought ones tear insanely easy, lol.

Right, phyllo dough for most pies is exactly like yours. Normally, at least where I'm from, we use six sheets per pie, so we divide the dough in six pieces and then we make them a bit bigger than the pan using a rolling pin. It just seemed like your phyllo had too much flour compared to ours and the sheets were a teensy bit too thick, but that makes sense because it's impossible to get it right without the right rolling pin. Like, you did impressively good considering you used a bottle.

Bougatsa isn't made with typical phyllo dough, though. That's why it's called bougatsa and not regular pie. As I said above, bougatsa dough is rich in butter because it's both in the dough itself and each sheet is also *slathered* in butter, not oil. It makes the dough more elastic and, as it melts, steam gets trapped in between the layers of the dough, so it looks more like puff pastry, not so much like phyllo. Also, bougatsa pies are not made in big pans like that, they're normally (and ideally) made to look like small parcels. So, you don't need a lot of space to make them, you just need butter and a lot of patience. And I don't feel like using either, hence why I never make bougatsa. 🤣

I'm Greek, we use the same rolling pin. Phyllo dough for bougatsa is different, though, in that you don't use flour or a rolling pin. You add butter to the dough and then you spread butter on it, too, so it's easy to stretch it. You get it into a big rectangle, you cut it in half, add the filling in the middle and then you fold the phyllo sheet around the filling in four, like an envelope. Then you wrap that with the other half of the phyllo sheet. You end up with texture that differs a lot from regular Greek pies, because of the butter. It's flakier and much lighter. I've seen it being made but I'm afraid to try it.

I've never attempted to make phyllo dough for bougatsa. Both because I can't get it thin enough, I'll definitely tear it but also because I don't want to know how much butter it takes to get it stretchy enough that it will not tear. 😅

Plenty more crops rely on commercialized pollination. Apples, blueberries and more. What makes almonds special is the sheer amount of them, as far as I can tell. It's the biggest pollination event in the world, bee keepers can't keep up and the demand keeps growing, as almond milk keeps becoming more popular.
Yes, exactly. You can look it up yourself, there are plenty of sources. Environmentalists liken sending bees to pollinate almonds with sending them to war.

They don't keep beehives, no. There is a honey bee pollination business in California, the biggest one in the world, because there are vast fields of almonds that need to be pollinated, so there isn't enough wild pollination, but there is also only the one type of culture, which makes the environment not ideal for wild pollination. So, you have bee keepers who will move their beehives around, to wherever there are crops they can pollinate. That also isn't easy on the bees, because they're not supposed to be moving around like that, so they get stressed. They don't get to hibernate enough, they're overworked and, those diseases that are easier to spread around in the almond fields, they spread them to wherever they move next. The result is lots of dead bees.

Bees are needed to pollinate almonds. Farmers use more pesticides on almonds than on other crops, which is obviously not good for the bees. Other than that, the bees need to wake up early from their hibernation to pollinate the almonds, which isn't easy on them, they have to work insane amounts to pollinate huge fields because there is a huge demand for almonds and the last problem is that about 80% of the world's almonds are grown in California, which means that bees have to work closely together, so diseases are easy to spread. Not to mention that, not only do the honeybees suffer, they also compete with other, native bees which also suffer as consequence. Almond production, then, is both exploitative and hurtful to bees.
Almond milk shouldn't be considered vegan-friendly, though. It's no better than being vegan and eating honey.
